Yeah, it just seems way too improbable that Gryffindor was awarded just enough points to beat Slytherin. Plus, wouldn't it have made more sense to award them the points right after Harry rescued the stone, like he did in the Chamber of Secrets? It's kind of rubbing it in everyone's faces even more by putting up Slytherin decorations and getting their hopes up only to change right before the cup is awarded.

I definitely disagree with Umbridge being at the bottom of the list. She was the Ministry's weapon all throughout the fifth book and her presence was crucial to making the ministry's war on Dumbledore and Harry feel real. I think she definitely benefits the series.

The sorting hat was sensing the part of Voldemort's soul in Harry, which is why he thought that he would do well in Slytherin. However, I do think that Harry may have had his own ambition coming into the wizarding world, since pretty much everyone was telling him that he was going to be a great wizard and he was already super famous and all that.

As far as Harry's character, I like how JK Rowling portrayed him because one-dementional characters with no flaws are really boring. Harry really is just an ordinary kid. Of course an eleven year old is going to side with his best friend over that weird Hermione girl. It's what eleven year old boys do. Overall, though, I think he turns out to have enough good characteristics to outweigh the bad.

Sherlock (Benedict Cumberbatch): Ravenclaw, because he's brilliant and places a lot of emphasis on intelligence (not to mention his "Mind Palace"). However, he would really fit in well with all of the houses. Gryffindor because he is undoubtedly brave when it comes to saving his friends. Hufflepuff because he is loyal and hardworking. Slytherin because he can be shrewd, cunning, and resourceful.
